title.en: Language work for Wisdom Paves the Way: noun forms, modals, stress and a complaint letter
Words with more than one job

text.en: The story of the clever sages and the king gives us words that change shape, words with two meanings, small verbs that carry big ideas, and a way of writing a letter that gets problems fixed.

Many verbs have noun forms. Deduce becomes deduction, observe becomes observation, scrutinise becomes scrutiny, accuse becomes accusation and recognise becomes recognition. Use the noun form when a noun is needed, as in 'a false accusation'.
Expressions carry meanings beyond the words. With all our hearts means with complete sincerity, to be precise means exact and accurate, taken aback means surprised, and erupts in applause means starts cheering together. More than meets the eye means hidden information that is not obvious.
Some words have several meanings. Face can be a noun, the front part of the head, or a verb, to deal with a difficult situation or to turn towards something. Bear can be an animal, or a verb meaning to tolerate, to accept, or to produce fruit or give birth.
Modal verbs such as may, might, can, could, must, should, shall and need to express functions. Can shows ability and may or might show possibility. Must shows necessity or a logical conclusion, and should shows suggestion or advice.
Shall can give a command, 'You shall come with me'. Would can show an imagined possibility. 'May your wisdom shine' is a wish, and 'we ought to be united' is moral obligation or advice.
How you stress a word changes the meaning of a sentence. In 'Look there, friends' stressing look, there or friends points the listener to a different idea. Practise a sentence by stressing a different word each time and say what changes.
A formal complaint letter follows a set format. The first paragraph states the purpose of writing and the problem. The next gives details and the effect on people, such as accidents or mosquitoes from stagnant water. The last asks politely for action. Use phrases like 'I would like to bring to your attention'.

problem.en: Fill in the blanks with the right noun form and modal verb: (a) She received an award in ___ (recognise) of her work. (b) You ___ listen more than you speak (suggestion). (c) A camel with a long tail ___ have driven off the pests (imagined possibility).

text.en: (a) recognition. The noun form of recognise is recognition.

why.en: A noun is needed after in.

text.en: (b) should. Should expresses suggestion or advice.
(c) would. Would have + past participle shows an imagined, hypothetical possibility.

prompt.en: Explain two things: how changing the stressed word changes a sentence, and what the first paragraph of a complaint letter must contain.

requiredIdeas.en: Stress points to the key idea: a different word stressed means a different meaning
The first paragraph states the purpose and the problem
Use formal polite language and a request for action

commonMisconceptions.en: Starting the letter with a long story

points.en: Learn noun forms: observe-observation, accuse-accusation, recognise-recognition.
Words like face and bear have several meanings.
Modal verbs show ability, possibility, necessity, advice, command and wish.
A complaint letter states the problem, gives details and asks for action.
